question: Why does the presence of knowledge not make objects inherently knowable?
premises: A cloth does not acquire the form of a pot even when the pot's features exist.
Knowledge inheres in the knower, not in external objects.
An object does not take on a nature that belongs elsewhere.
inference: Even when knowledge is present in the knower, objects do not thereby possess knowability as their own nature.
plain_english: A cloth does not take on the form of a pot with a broad base and so on. In the same way, even when knowledge is present in the knower, objects do not thereby become knowable by their own nature.
